Jatayu.description: A humorous and somewhat naive writer of thrillers and friend of Feluda, whose real name is Lalmohan Ganguli.

Peter Robertson.description: A British visitor interested in Indian culture and a descendant of Patrick Robertson, who originally took the ruby.

David McCutcheon.description: A European professor who has conducted extensive research on the temples of Birbhum.

Patrick Robertson.description: An ancestor of Peter Robertson, who fought in the mutiny and took the ruby from India.

Shatadal Sen.description: A school friend of Lalmohan Babu and a professor of history at Vishwa Bharati in Santiniketan.

Birbhum.description: A district in West Bengal, India, known for its unique rock formations and terracotta temples.

Abhijaan.description: A Bengali film referenced in the conversation, possibly evoking the 'Mama-Bhagney' rocks.

Tagore.description: Refers to Rabindranath Tagore, the Nobel laureate poet who spent many years in Santiniketan.

The Sahara Shivers.description: A fictional thriller written by Lalmohan Babu.

Santiniketan.description: Santiniketan, sometimes spelled Santikiniketan, is a town in Birbhum, famous for being the home of Tagore and the location of Vishwa Bharati University, known for its artistic heritage.

Bakreshwar.description: A place in Birbhum known for its hot springs.

Kenduli.description: A village in Birbhum, famous as the birthplace of the poet Jaydev and for its annual fair.

Jaydev.description: A celebrated medieval poet, believed to have been born in Kenduli.

Tarapeeth.description: A temple town in Birbhum, famous for the Tarapith temple and the tantrik Bama Khepa.

Bama Khepa.description: A famous tantrik saint who lived in Tarapeeth.

Dubrajpur.description: A town in Birbhum, known for its unusual rock formations.

Bengal.description: A region in eastern India, of which Birbhum is a part.

Robertson’s Ruby.description: A legendary ruby taken from India by Patrick Robertson, now being returned by his descendant.

Lucknow.description: A city in northern India, significant in the context of the mutiny.

Bengal regiment.description: A British Indian Army regiment mentioned in the context of the mutiny.

nawab.description: A title for a Muslim ruler or nobleman in South Asia.

Bolpur.description: A town near Santiniketan, serving as a gateway to the area.

Santiniketan Express.description: A train that runs to Bolpur, known for its special Lounge Car.

Burdwan.description: A town in West Bengal, where the Santiniketan Express stops.

Vishwa Bharati.description: A prestigious university in Santiniketan, founded by Tagore.

Calcutta.description: The former name of Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal.

Howrah.description: A major railway station in Kolkata.

Ambassador.description: A classic Indian car model, often used as taxis or private vehicles.

Mama-Bhagney.description: A Bengali phrase meaning 'uncle and nephew', often used to describe a specific rock formation.

dhobi.description: A traditional Indian washerman or laundryman.

mela.description: A fair or festival, typically large and held annually.

hauls.description: Likely a typographical error for 'bauls', referring to wandering minstrels of Bengal.

woollens.description: Warm clothing, especially sweaters and jackets, commonly used in Indian English.

Charminar.description: A popular Indian brand of cigarettes.

Calcutta Museum.description: A major museum in Calcutta (now Kolkata), likely referring to the Indian Museum, one of the oldest and largest museums in India.

Delhi.description: The capital city of India, often referenced as the seat of government and administrative decisions.

England.description: A country in the United Kingdom, referenced as the place where the ruby was valued.

The Statesman.description: The Statesman is a prominent English-language newspaper published in India.

Britain.description: Refers to the United Kingdom, the home country of Tom Maxwell's ancestors.

Webley Scott.description: A British firearms manufacturer, known for producing revolvers.

Africa.description: A continent mentioned as a place where Tom Maxwell has traveled and used his revolver.

maharajas.description: Indian princes or kings, historically rulers of princely states.

chaiwalla.description: A vendor who sells tea, commonly found at railway stations and streets in India.

rickshaws.description: Three-wheeled passenger carts, either cycle or auto, commonly used for transportation in India.

Kishorilal.description: Kishorilal Dandania, also called Kishori, is the son of G.L. Dandania who greets the visitors at the house and wishes to start his own business rather than join his father's.

Inspector Chaubey.description: A police inspector and friend of Mr. Dandania, whose full name is Richard Shankar Prasad and whose father was Charles Premchand.

Uttarayan.description: A residential complex or area the group visits, noted for its unique architecture.

Pearson Palli.description: A locality mentioned as a way to find Mr Sen's house.

Hetampur.description: A nearby location known for its terracotta temples.

Udichi.description: A building or house in Uttarayan, admired for its beauty.

Shyamali.description: Another building in Uttarayan, also noted for its beauty.

Santhal.description: Santhals are an indigenous tribal community in India, known for their distinct culture and dances; the group visits a Santhal village.

Benaras.description: Also known as Varanasi, a historic city in India, referenced for its religious significance.

Salar Jung.description: Refers to the Salar Jung Museum in Hyderabad, known for its private collection.

Hyderabad.description: A major city in southern India, home to the Salar Jung Museum.

Ganesh Dandania Museum.description: A proposed private museum by Mr Dandania for the ruby.

antakshari.description: A popular Indian spoken parlor game involving singing songs in turns.

sharbat.description: A sweet, flavored drink popular in South Asia.

inke liye mithai aur sharbat mangwao.description: Hindi for 'send for sweets and sherbet for them'.

Ganesh Dandania.description: A wealthy and somewhat shady businessman from Dubrajpur who is suspected of being involved in the ruby mystery.

Reginald Maxwell.description: A professional photographer and friend of Peter Robertson with ancestral ties to India, specifically related to an ancestor who killed Hiralal.

Jagannath Chatterjee.description: A historian specializing in the temples of Birbhum, who offers his expertise to Peter.

Hanuman.description: A Hindu god, revered as a monkey deity and a central figure in the Ramayana.

Mount Gandhamadan.description: A mythical mountain in Hindu mythology, associated with Hanuman's legendary feats.

Ram.description: A major deity in Hinduism, protagonist of the Ramayana, known for building a bridge to Lanka.

Kali.description: A prominent Hindu goddess associated with power and destruction, often worshipped in temples.

Bihar.description: A state in eastern India, mentioned as Inspector Chaubey's place of origin.

puja.description: A Hindu ritual of worship, often performed in temples or homes.

lakhs.description: A unit in the Indian numbering system equal to one hundred thousand (100,000).

tubewell.description: A type of well in which a long pipe is bored into the ground to access groundwater, commonly used in India.

Chandu Mallik.description: Chandu Mallik is a local goonda (thug) who threatens Tom after a confrontation at the cremation ground and is a suspect who was at a dance and later with friends at the time of the incident.

Maharani of Burdwan.description: A historical queen from the princely state of Burdwan in Bengal, credited with building the temple at Kenduli.

Ramayana.description: An ancient Indian epic that narrates the life of Prince Rama, with its stories often depicted in temple carvings.

Mahabharata.description: One of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, detailing the Kurukshetra War and the fates of the Kaurava and Pandava princes.

India.description: The country where the story is set, with references to its culture, independence, and social conditions.

bauls.description: Mystic minstrels from Bengal known for their distinctive music and spiritual songs.

banyan.description: A type of large fig tree native to India, often serving as a gathering place in villages.

ektara.description: A one-stringed musical instrument commonly used by folk musicians in Bengal.

pyre.description: A pile of wood on which a dead body is burned as part of Hindu funeral rites.

goonda.description: A Hindi term for a thug or criminal, often used to describe local troublemakers.

sahib.description: A term of respect or address for a man, especially used during the British colonial period in India.

punkha-puller.description: A servant employed to operate a punkha, a large manual fan used in colonial India.

Rev. Pritchard.description: A historical figure and author who adopted Anant Narayan and wrote about the Maxwell family history.

Hiralal.description: A punkha-puller who was killed by Maxwell in the story recounted from the past.

Anant Narayan.description: The orphaned son of Hiralal, later adopted by Rev. Pritchard and converted to Christianity.

Mr Naskar.description: A well-known businessman from Calcutta who serves as a local host for the group.

Phulberey.description: A village mentioned as the location for the Santhal dance.

Soubhagya Kunda.description: A pond near the temples, whose name means 'good fortune' in Bengali.

Lancashire.description: A county in North West England, cited as the origin of Peter and Tom.

bearer.description: A domestic servant, often in charge of serving food and drinks in Indian households.

Tapesh.description: Feluda's cousin, loyal assistant, and the narrator of the stories, affectionately known as Topshe.

Dr Sinha.description: A local doctor called to examine Tom after he was attacked.

National Geographic.description: A renowned international magazine known for its photography and exploration assignments.

beedi.description: A thin, hand-rolled cigarette made from tobacco wrapped in a leaf, commonly smoked in India.

Babu.description: A respectful term for a gentleman, often used in Bengali to address educated men.

paisa.description: A unit of currency in India, traditionally a fraction of a rupee.

Baikuntha Mallik.description: Lalmohan Babu's favorite poet, known for writing about Santiniketan.

Kopai.description: A river in West Bengal, admired by Tagore and featured in local poetry.

Goalpara.description: A village by the river Kopai, visited by the characters.

hypnotized.description: A trance-like state induced by hypnosis, sometimes used in detective fiction to reveal hidden truths.

Sandesh.description: A Bengali children's magazine revived by Satyajit Ray, where the first Feluda story was published.

Felu.description: Felu, whose real name is Prodosh C. Mitter and often respectfully called Felu Babu or Mr Mitter, is the sharp and inquisitive protagonist detective of the stories.

Penguin Books.description: The publishing house responsible for this edition of the book.

Gurgaon.description: A city in Haryana, India, mentioned as the location of Penguin Books India's office.

Haryana.description: An Indian state where Gurgaon is located.

London.description: The city where Penguin Books Ltd has its registered offices.

Dublin.description: The capital city of Ireland, mentioned as a location of Penguin Ireland.

Melbourne.description: A city in Australia, mentioned as a location of Penguin Group (Australia).

Auckland.description: A city in New Zealand, mentioned as a location of Penguin Group (NZ).

Johannesburg.description: A city in South Africa, mentioned as a location of Penguin Books (South Africa).

Satyajit Ray.description: The author of the Feluda stories, a renowned Indian filmmaker and writer.

da.description: A Bengali suffix meaning 'elder brother', used as a term of respect and affection.

dada.description: A Bengali word meaning 'elder brother', from which the suffix 'da' is derived.

punkha.description: A manually operated fan, often used in colonial India to provide ventilation.
